docs.title: Git Workflow
docs.text: This page describes the Git workflow adopted for MUSICO software development, with a focus on the use of bare repositories.

docs.title: Bare Repository
docs.text:
A bare repository is a Git repository that contains only the version-control data (the contents of a normal .git/ directory) with no working tree. It is created with:

git init --bare <repo-name>.git

Because it holds no checked-out files, a bare repository is designed exclusively to receive and serve commits — it is never edited directly.

docs.title: Why MUSICO Uses Bare Repositories
docs.text: Concern Bare repository behaviour Central server storage No working-tree files means no accidental edits on the server and a smaller footprint. Multi-developer push/pull Bare repositories accept git push from any number of clients without the "refusing to update checked-out branch" error that a normal repository produces. CI/CD integration Deployment hooks (post-receive, post-update) fire reliably after every push, letting the server automatically build or deploy the MUSICO software without manual intervention. Backup and mirroring A bare clone (git clone --mirror) reproduces every ref exactly, making it the correct form for backup targets and read-only mirrors.

docs.title: Key Differences: Bare vs. Normal Repository
docs.text: Feature Normal repository Bare repository Working tree Yes No .git/ subdirectory Yes Contents are at root Direct file editing Yes Not applicable Accepts git push Restricted Yes Intended use Development workstation Central server / remote

docs.title: Typical Directory Layout
docs.text:
/srv/git/
└── musico.git/          ← bare repository (central server)
    ├── HEAD
    ├── config
    ├── description
    ├── hooks/
    │   └── post-receive  ← deployment automation
    ├── info/
    ├── objects/
    └── refs/

Developer workstations clone from the bare repository and push changes back to it:

Developer A  ──push/pull──┐
Developer B  ──push/pull──┼──► /srv/git/musico.git  (bare)
Developer C  ──push/pull──┘

docs.title: Setting Up a Bare Repository
docs.text:
On the server:

# initialise a new bare repository
git init --bare /srv/git/musico.git

# or mirror an existing repository
git clone --mirror <existing-remote-url> /srv/git/musico.git

On a developer machine:

# clone from the bare repository
git clone <user>@<server>:/srv/git/musico.git musico

# add it as a remote in an existing local repo
git remote add origin <user>@<server>:/srv/git/musico.git

docs.title: post-receive Hook Example
docs.text:
Place an executable script at /srv/git/musico.git/hooks/post-receive to trigger automated actions after every push:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Deploy to the staging environment after every push to main
while read oldrev newrev refname; do
    if [ "$refname" = "refs/heads/main" ]; then
        echo "Deploying MUSICO to staging..."
        GIT_WORK_TREE=/opt/musico/staging git checkout -f main
    fi
done

Make it executable:

chmod +x /srv/git/musico.git/hooks/post-receive

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
This section walks through the day-to-day workflow for a MUSICO developer: cloning the central repository, making changes, and pushing them back.

The paths used throughout:

Role Path Central (bare) repository /workspace_hdd/MUSICO/software Your local working copy /home/username/musico

Replace username with your actual system username.

docs.title: Step 1 — Clone the Repository
docs.text:
Clone the central bare repository into your personal working folder. The destination path is independent of where the bare repository lives on the server.

git clone /workspace_hdd/MUSICO/software /home/username/musico

This creates a full local copy of the project history inside /home/username/musico/, which is where you will do all your editing.

Move into the folder before running any further Git commands:

cd /home/username/musico

docs.title: Step 2 — Develop and Commit Locally
docs.text:
Edit, create, or delete files inside your working folder as normal. When you reach a logical checkpoint, record the changes in the local repository.

Stage the files you want to include in the commit:

# stage a specific file
git add src/mymodule.py

# stage all changes in the current directory
git add .

Commit the staged changes with a short, descriptive message:

git commit -m "Add initial signal processing module"

The commit is saved to your local repository only — nothing has reached the central server yet. You can make as many local commits as you need before pushing.

docs.title: Step 3 — Push to the Central Repository
docs.text:
When your work is ready to share, push your commits back to /workspace_hdd/MUSICO/software:

git push origin master

If the central repository uses main as the default branch, substitute main for master.

Pull before you push

Always pull in any changes that teammates may have pushed since your last sync before pushing, to avoid conflicts:

git pull origin master
git push origin master

A complete single-session cycle looks like this:

clone (once)  →  edit files  →  git add  →  git commit  →  git pull  →  git push
                     ↑_______________|  (repeat for each logical change)

docs.title: 1. Inspect the Commit Log
docs.text:
git log

Shows the full commit history — author, date, and message for every commit. Useful flags:

--oneline : Condenses each commit to a single line (short hash + message). Good for a quick overview.

--graph : Draws an ASCII branch/merge graph to the left of each entry.

--all : Includes commits on every branch, not just the currently checked-out one.

Combined example:

git log --oneline --graph --all

docs.title: 2. List Files Under the master Branch
docs.text:
To see every file tracked at the tip of master without checking it out:

git ls-tree -r --name-only master

-r : Recurses into subdirectories so all files at every depth are listed.

--name-only : Prints just the file paths, omitting blob hashes and mode bits.

For a bare repository on the server this is the standard way to browse the file tree, since there is no working directory to ls through.

docs.title: 3. Check the Current Status of Your Working Tree
docs.text:
git status

Reports which files are staged for the next commit, which are modified but not yet staged, and which are completely untracked. Run this before any git add or git commit to avoid committing unintended changes.

docs.title: 4. See Exactly What Changed Before Committing
docs.text:
git diff

Shows the line-by-line difference between your working tree and the last commit. To compare only what is already staged:

git diff --staged

This lets you review your changes one more time before they become part of the project history.
